# TConstruct LAN component fixture

`cases.json` supplies SNBT stack inputs for the generic host encode/decode tests. The generated pickaxe is the unchanged earlier Creative output; the second case adds representative valid TConstruct fields and presentation components synthetically. It is a transport fixture, not a claim that those upgrades were naturally applied or that the augmented combination is valid gameplay. The vanilla control carries a non-unit count.

For each case, round-trip through the host-to-guest and guest-to-host paths using the target host's actual item and registry mappings. Assert the same item, count, damage and all components, including nested material IDs, attack/mining stats, mining rules, upgrades and overslime, as well as lore and item model. No component may occur twice. Ordinary vanilla stacks and unrelated custom data must stay intact. Also test a server-origin wire patch, preserving unknown/removed components where the host supports it, and save/reload as separate checks.

The old TConstruct hooks appended `custom_data`, lore and item model and cancelled the host wrappers; they have been removed in favor of the host wrappers and PlutoLib transport bundle. The independent library demo passed representative LAN and save/reconnect checks, while this TConstruct fixture has only been checked through parsing and item NBT. The combined TConstruct runtime and dedicated-server behavior are not established.

## Material durability and mining acceptance

For `generated_pickaxe`, the source-generated stack has `minecraft:max_damage = 60` and a matching `tic_max_damage = 60`. Its `minecraft:tool` has `damage_per_block = 1`, default speed `1.0`, a wood-tier incorrect-for-drops rule, and an effective-pickaxe rule with speed `2.0` and `correct_for_drops = true`; `tic_mining_tool` contains the same rule data. These values describe this fixture, not every material or block. The augmented case intentionally mixes synthetic fields and is only a transport oracle, not an expected Haste or Jagged speed.

Loss of the real components can leave the guest with a different per-stack maximum or missing tool rules. This may affect the damage bar, advanced durability information, mining prediction, speed, correct-tool checks or drops depending on the host path and registered item defaults; it has not yet been shown in a live game. TConstruct also keeps `tic_max_damage` and a copy of mining rules in custom data, and existing hooks read those values. Those fallbacks can mask a missing real component, so matching appearance or one successful mine is not sufficient proof of a complete wire round trip. Some current Horizon UI and item paths read item defaults rather than per-stack components; retaining the component alone is not proof those paths use it.

Representative acceptance after the common codec fix: place the generated stack in a guest inventory through the host, check both real components and the copied fields, damage it through an ordinary action, and compare the remaining durability/bar and any advanced tooltip with the authoritative host. Mine a block matching the effective-pickaxe rule and verify the actual speed and drop behavior against the same host stack; separately check a block rejected by the fixture's wood-tier rule. Send the stack back guest-to-host, save and reload, and recheck the values and operation. Use a disposable world and identify granted materials or command fixtures. The unmodified vanilla count control must also remain unchanged. This is a planned representative check, not a completed LAN or gameplay result.
